30 A slice of germanium of cross-sectional area 1.0 cm2 carries a current of 56 µA. The number
density of charge carriers in the germanium is 2.0 × 1013
cm–3. Each charge carrier has a charge
equal to the charge on an electron.
slice of
germanium
area 1.0 cm2
current
56 µA
What is the average drift velocity of the charge carriers in the germanium?
A
0.18 m s–1
B
18 m s–1
C
180 m s–1
D
1800 m s–1

hints: Notice the units given: area is $1.0$ $\text{cm}^2$, number density is $2.0 \times 10^{13}$ $\text{cm}^{-3}$, but current is $56$ $\mu\text{A}$ and drift velocity is asked in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
Recall $I = nAvq$ for drift velocity, where $q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ $\text{C}$ and $n$ and $A$ must both be in $\text{m}^{-3}$ and $\text{m}^2$.
walkthrough: Identify the governing relation $I = nAvq$, so $v = I/(nAq)$ for the $56$ $\mu\text{A}$ current through area $1.0$ $\text{cm}^2$.
Convert current to SI: $I = 56$ $\mu\text{A} = 56 \times 10^{-6}$ $\text{A}$ and charge to $q = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ $\text{C}$.
Rounded to two significant figures this is $0.18$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$. This is option A.

A.explanation: Gives $v \approx 0.18$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$ from $v = I/(nAq)$ after correct conversion to $\text{m}^2$ and $\text{m}^{-3}$.

B.explanation: About 100 times too large, from failing to convert both $1.0$ $\text{cm}^2$ and $2.0 \times 10^{13}$ $\text{cm}^{-3}$ consistently to SI units.

C.explanation: About 1000 times too large, from using $n$ in $\text{cm}^{-3}$ and $A$ in $\text{cm}^2$ directly with $I$ in $\text{A}$.

D.explanation: About 10000 times too large, from a larger combined power-of-ten error in the $\text{cm}$ to $\text{m}$ conversions.
